en: Draw an uncertainty band around the predicted islands, because errors in today's velocity grow when they are multiplied by 50 million years.
Put a scale bar on the predicted map so a reader can see how many kilometers the method moved the blocks, not only a pretty new outline.
One student gathers GNSS rates, one converts units, one draws arrows, and one writes uncertainties, a division of labor that matches the method.
The competency is about position and shape of the crust, so the method should not wander into guessing 50-million-year rainfall or cities.
State that treating the Philippines as one rigid plate is an approximation; GNSS already shows internal deformation that a careful method includes.
Finish the prediction with because: the islands should sit farther along today's vectors because we multiplied measured velocity by geologic time.
To identify crash-protection devices, gather crash-test reports from agencies such as NHTSA or your local transport office, then name seatbelts, airbags, and crumple zones.
Secondary safety sources also name head restraints that limit neck snap in a rear collision, another way to reduce impact effects besides the three famous devices.
Car-safety papers describe side-impact beams in doors that spread a T-bone crash force, a sourced device that protects occupants from the side.
A collapsible steering column is designed to shorten in a frontal crash so the wheel does less harm to the driver's chest, a device named in engineering sources.
Child seats and booster seats, described in LTO and pediatric safety pages, reduce collision impact on small bodies that adult belts do not fit well.
Some vehicle standards require softer, more crumple-friendly fronts so a collision with a pedestrian delivers less peak force, a source-backed design choice.
Laminated windshields that stay in one sheet are cited as reducing ejection and cutting injuries, another sourced way collisions do less harm.
WHO also documents motorcycle helmets as impact reducers for riders, a sourced example outside cars that still fits reducing collision harm.
Transport agencies publish that a belt only reduces impact if it is worn; reminder chimes in source specs exist because unused belts cannot help.
Crash-test sources warn that airbags are designed to work with a seatbelt, so gathering 'ways' should present them as a pair, not as rivals.
Engineering sources define a crumple zone as a designed crush space in front or rear, not random damage, so the cabin decelerates over a longer time.
Local transport pages may discuss seatbelts on buses or jeepneys; gather whether those rules exist, because reducing impact is not only for private cars.
If a source does not state a percent reduction, do not invent one; name the device and the agency, which is enough for the competency.
Interior padding on dashboards, listed in safety standards, is another sourced way to lengthen contact time and lower peak force in a crash.
The Philippine archipelago sits where the Philippine Sea Plate meets the Eurasian Plate, so both plates control where the islands go.
A plate's velocity is its speed and its direction together, so predicting the future needs both, not just how fast the plate moves.
On the western side, the Manila Trench swallows the other plate, so the whole archipelago is squeezed between two converging plates.
The same plate motion that builds mountains and feeds volcanoes today is the motion that will carry the archipelago to a new position.
Satellites send signals to ground stations on the islands, and the tiny yearly shifts in those signals reveal the plate's true velocity.
Fifty million years is far longer than all of human history, so even a slow crawl of centimeters per year adds up to an enormous distance.
New volcanoes may rise and old islands may sink, so the 50-million-year archipelago will likely have a different lineup of islands than today.
If a car keeps driving at a steady speed, you can predict where it will be later; the same math predicts where the Philippine Plate will be in 50 million years.
The 50-million-year map is called a model because it uses today's measurements and stated assumptions, not a guaranteed future.
Classification stacks: humans are mammals because of milk and hair, and primates because of forward eyes and grasping hands, not one label alone.
